headline: Capturing the boat thieves
summary: Far downriver, north of Elkhorn, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow find their stolen boat and catch the three thieves completely off guard. Rifles leveled, Roosevelt orders hands up, and the men surrender without a shot. Earlier he brings down a whitetail doe at 75 yards.

events.detail: Shoots a whitetail doe at 75 yards
Surprises and captures the three men who stole the Elkhorn boat, with no shots fired

tr_quotes.text: Shot white tail doe; 75 yards. Captured the three boat-theives. We took them absolutely by surprise.

As they knew there was no other boat on the river but the one they had taken, and as they had not thought of our building another, they were completely taken unawares, one with his rifle on the ground, and the others with theirs on their shoulders; so there was no fight, nor any need of pluck on our part. . . I told them to throw up their hands, they saw that we had the drop on them completely, and I guess they also saw that we surely meant shooting if they hesitated, and so their hands went up at once.

uncertain: The thieves' names come from the April 2 entry. The source gives the distance downstream as about 100 miles; the longer quotation is TR's later account, cited from Hagedorn.

headline: Guarding prisoners on an icy river
summary: With the captives aboard both boats, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow start the slow trip back toward Medora until an ice jam stops them. The prisoners cannot be tied up for fear of frostbite, and supplies dwindle until only flour is left. To pass the long watches, Roosevelt reads Anna Karenina cover to cover.

events.detail: Heads back upriver toward Medora with the prisoners in two boats until ice blocks the way

Reads all of Tolstoy's Anna Karenina during the trek

tr_quotes.text: Came on with our prisoners till hung up by ice-jam.

uncertain: The source labels the third prisoner with an ethnic epithet before the surname Burnsted; only the surname is used here. The food shortage and reading span several days.
